# Education in Norway
Organized education in Norway dates back to around 2000 B.C., with cathedral schools founded in the 12th century to educate priests. After the 1537 Reformation and Norway’s union with Denmark, Latin schools became mandatory in market towns. Compulsory reading training began in 1736, evolving into the "folkeskole" primary school in 1827, which was compulsory for seven years from 1889 and extended to nine years in 1969. The folkeskole was replaced by the "grunnskole" (foundation school) in the 1970s–1980s. Since the 2003 Independent Schools Act, private schools must have an internationally recognized curriculum or an alternative pedagogical or religious approach, are government-approved and heavily grant-aided, and cannot select students based on ability.
Today, the Norwegian school system comprises three parts: elementary school (barneskole, ages 6–12), lower secondary school (ungdomsskole, ages 13–16), both compulsory as "grunnskole," and upper secondary school (videregående skole, ages 16–19). At barneskole, students focus on foundational skills and social learning without official grades; grading begins in ungdomsskole, where academic performance influences upper secondary school placement. Upper secondary education, mostly public, offers general and vocational tracks with completion rates around 73%. Teachers’ roles vary by qualifications, from preschool teachers with bachelor’s degrees to university-educated lecturers. Higher education includes universities, university colleges, and private institutions, with admissions based on grades and specific certifications. Norway uses multiple grading systems, with recent transitions aligned with the Bologna process. The academic year runs from mid-August to June, with regular vacations and national holidays. Special education focuses on inclusive learning environments within local schools, supported by specialist services.
